The latest Nvidia driver update has reportedly introduced a nasty bug thatâs causing excessive SSD writing on usersâ machines, resulting in data being continuously recorded at a staggering 25,000 percent increase, and rapidly degrading peopleâs hardware in the process.

As reported by TroubleGrid, the 621.24 Nvidia GeForce Game Ready Driver update went live on November 12, and reports of its odd effects on usersâ machines trickled in shortly after. In simple terms, a bug introduced in the update is causing the NVDisplay.Container.exe to continuously write large amounts of data to some usersâ SSDs.

While the bug might also have an impact on your PCâs performance, the main issue is that SSDs slowly degrade every time data is recorded on them. Usually, this isnât really a problem, as most SSDs should last around 10 years before they fully fall to bits. However, the error introduced in Nvidiaâs 621.24 update isâand this is not an exaggerationâcausing some usersâ solid state drives to continuously write data at over 250 times the normal rate, and thus reducing their lifespan 250 times faster.

The problem appears to be quite widespread too, with users on r/pcgaming, r/pcmasterrace, and pretty much every PC-centric subreddit reporting that theyâve been hit with the bug. Funnily enough, my PC has been acting real weird the past few days, so I decided to run a check that one user on r/pcmasterrace suggested.

Comment byu/HLumin from discussion inpcmasterrace

I restarted my PC, left it idle for a while, and ran the command in PowerShell. While my SSD doesnât seem to have been hit quite as badly as others, yeah, it sure as shit wasnât writing over 30 GB of data to my SSD for absolutely no goddamn reason this time last week.

Thankfully, the fix is simple: revert to the previous Nvidia driver update. I did exactly that and, hey, all of a sudden, the same process is only writing about 4.5 MB of data to my SSD. Gee, thanks, Nvidia.

By the way, this update is over a week old at this point, and this is a very well-reported problemâhow the hell has this not been fixed yet? Also, when is Nvidia gonna post me the check for my new SSD? Now that Jensen is gone, it can be taken out of the leather jacket budget.

More importantly, though, how did such a massive bug like this slip through the cracks? Users on Reddit have two theories: either Nvidia wants to destroy our SSDs on purpose so we buy more at overly inflated prices (rather unlikely), or more compellingly, it could have something to do with the fact that Jensen proudly admitted in May that Nvidia is requiring that its engineers use vast numbers of AI tokens in all aspects of their work.

Bizarrely, AMDâs driver update introduced a very similar bug last week, but AMD rolled out a fix pretty sharpish and the issue no longer remains.

David Fincher and Quentin Tarantino prove a perfect match in this Once Upon A Time in… Hollywood spin-off that centers Brad Pitt's Oscar-winning stuntman. Does it need to exist? Not really. But we're glad it does.

Fincher knows how to direct Tarantino's peerless dialogue

Pitt's as good here as he was in …Hollywood.

Rick Dalton's absence is awkwardly handled

Why you can trust GamesRadar+ Our experts review games, movies and tech over countless hours, so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about our reviews policy.

A Netflix sequel to 2019's Once Upon A Time in… Hollywood that drops Rick Dalton and Sharon Tate for further Cliff Booth misadventures is an undeniably odd proposition. But this David Fincher-directed, Quentin Tarantino-written follow-up plays to both their strengths, and proves that Brad Pitt is never better than when working with his movie-making soulmates.

Unburdened from the self-inflicted pressure to make his tenth and final movie a career-capping magnum opus, this is Tarantino’s most playful and straightforwardly enjoyable script since Jackie Brown. In fact, there's a lot of Elmore Leonard in this late-70s Hollywood hangout movie that only occasionally detours into criminal activity; little surprise that Tarantino has also penned the novelization releasing next month.

Plot-light but chock-full of memorable scenes, exchanges and characters, it might not have the thematic depth of its predecessor, which explored the difficult transition to the Hollywood New Wave for outdated stars like Rick Dalton (and their stuntmen). Neither does it really reckon with OUATIH's revisionist fairytale ending by focusing so squarely on Cliff. But Pitt's ceaselessly cool, sociopathic alpha dude is a blast to be reacquainted with.

Set over a matter of days, some 8 years after averting a Manson Family massacre, Cliff is now back working odd jobs around L.A. after Rick upped sticks to Sydney for a starring role in the successful Aussie series Dingo Dan. Still something of a fixer for his friends, resourceful war hero Cliff is approached by A-list movie star Charlie Peters (Scott Caan, looking more like his dad by the day) not to double for him, but to solve a problem involving a pair of Filipino brothers whom Charlie has accidentally hired to murder his wife, Tony (Carla Gugino).

Release date: November 25 (IMAX), December 23 (Netflix)Available: In theaters and NetflixDirector: David FincherWriter: Quentin TarantinoRuntime: 2h 20m

Also central is Peters' agent, Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki) – an Aussie immigrant and former film critic who Cliff, of course, has the hots for. It's been a minute since a proper Tarantino romance (if you don't count Cliff and Rick's bromance in OUATIH), and Cliff's playful pursuit of kinky Karen fizzes like a classic Bogart and Bacall pairing. Former RoboCop Peter Weller is also something of a scene-stealer as Cliff's grumpy but loving dad.

What you might be wondering is what Fight Club director David Fincher brings to the table, and the answer is a lot. Like the peanut butter and chocolate pairing of Fincher and Sorkin on The Social Network, the two filmmaking titans operate surprisingly harmoniously here. Fincher's ice-cold technical precision is best exemplified in the depiction of the killer Verdusco brothers. One early home invasion sequence is shockingly brutal and recalls the matter-of-fact violence of Zodiac. While, like OUATIH, the movie builds to an explosive action set-piece that is ferocious, unforgettable and sends you out on a gleeful high.

Despite everything The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth has going for it, there is still a niggling sense that it's somewhat superfluous as an exercise. Would all this time, money and effort not be better spent on anything other than a side-story involving a Tarantino supporting character? As if to head off the accusation, Cliff at one point asks Karen, "You might be wondering, why all of it?" The answer: "I'm not that deep." And neither is the film. It's a romp, a caper, a good time that luxuriates in the texture of late 70s Hollywood but doesn't have an awful lot to say beyond 'Isn't this a great place to spend 140 minutes?'

Pitt's ceaselessly cool, sociopathic alpha dude is a blast to be reacquainted with.

There are some fun cameos to watch out for: Timothy Olyphant returns as Rick Dalton's old Bounty Law co-star, James Stacy, for a terrific scene that takes Tarantino back into Inglourious Basterds territory. And Caan makes an electric return to movies as A-lister Peters, whose voluminous ego overcompensates for his diminutive stature – a tragedy Caan was stuck on the Hawaii Five-0 reboot for a decade. But Yahya Abdul-Mateen II is underutilized as blacksploitation star Rodrick 'Hot Rod' Harrison, and Leonardo DiCaprio's Dalton is conspicuous by his absence; Tarantino's script is on shakiest ground when repeatedly trying to justify his nonappearance.

The beneficiary of Narnia's 3-month delay, The Further Mis-Adventures… is getting a two-week release on IMAX screens before it heads to Netflix. Despite my (limited) misgivings, the big(gest) screen is the format to seek out, as it's the type of film where full immersion relies on undivided attention. Plus, you'd be mad to pass up the opportunity to see a Fincher-directed, Erik Messerschmidt-shot movie on the best screen possible. Whether or not we'll get Tarantino's tenth and final movie anytime soon is unclear as the search continues for the perfect swan song. But, in the meantime, more Tarantino scripts making their way into the hands of filmmakers like David Fincher can only be a good thing.

The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth plays on IMAX screens for two weeks from November 25, and releases on Netflix from December 23. For more, here are the most exciting upcoming movies heading our way across the rest of the year, and beyond.

#3697. GTA 6 breaks the all-time livestream viewer record hours before it's available to play for most of the world

Hours before it's even playable in most of the world, Grand Theft Auto 6 has already broken the record for the most viewers across livestreaming platforms like Twitch.

According to streaming data and analytics website Streams Charts, GTA 6 had amassed 6.38m live viewers across Twitch, YouTube, and Kick at 12:30 UTC today. At that time, the game had been officially available for a few hours in New Zealand, and elsewhere by using a region-switch trick.

The previous record for most live viewers was set by Valorant, Riot Game's popular tactical shooter, during its closed beta in xx. That game brought in 1.74m live viewers, but it's worth noting there was a promotion offering players a chance to access the beta if they watched a stream. Despite having no such incentive, GTA 6 has more than tripled Valorant's record.

Twitch is the largest platform for GTA 6 streams according to Streams Charts, and already the game is the 6th biggest category in Twitch history. It's also expected the figure will increase as GTA 6 launches officially in more regions of the world.

I am nothing if not entirely predictable. I've waited 13 years to play a new Grand Theft Auto game and the first thing I do when I finally get around to booting GTA 6—and definitely not spoofing my home address to access it early—is jam a mouse and keyboard into my Xbox Series X just to see.

GTA 5, once it made its way to PC, was always a game I played both with a keyboard and mouse and with a controller plugged in. Keeb and rodent for shooting, especially in the first-person mode, and the controller for just getting about in the game world. It was a real best of both worlds kinda thing that the PC does so well.

It was the same with Red Dead Redemption 2, a game I completely avoided until it finally came to the PC. Keyboard and mouse for runnin' and gunnin' and a controller for horsin' around. Yeehaw.

So, I was hoping—hoping against hope, really—that I could just do the same with GTA 6. I was hoping that I could just plug in my little Mountain keyboard and my DeathAdder mouse, and it would just work.

Sadly no, there is no mouse and keyboard support for GTA 6. There is for Xbox, and my keyboard works fine just in the home screens, but as soon as you hit the game itself… nada. Keyboard and mouse support is still very much an occasional thing for Microsoft's console. It is supported, but it's on a per-game basis where devs have to actively code support into their Xbox versions of a title in order for a keyboard and mouse to work.

It's not actually that rare—some 450 games, and big games such as Cyberpunk 2077 and Alan Wake 2, have some level of support for one or both peripherals. But it is certainly not something Rockstar has spent any time putting in place when it was spending an extra year optimising the game after the delayed release. Which is a shame, given that the company has gone to great lengths to add a huge level of detail to its world to the point it almost feels like it's thought of everything.

More frustrating given that right now I bet there are Rockstar developers playing the game on keyboard and mouse in internal PC-only builds of the game. Would I have sacrificed sitting on my comfy sofa playing it writ large on my living room wall through my 4K projector just to sit at my desk with a keyboard and mouse? Maybe. It would have certainly felt like I was playing it on PC.

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

Something else Rockstar hasn't put into the game is any steering wheel control. Jacob, as a racing fan, tried to get his PlayStation wheelbase running on his PS5 copy of the game… but alas that is unsupported, too. Which was a source of frustration for him as he co-opted his partner in carrying his sim rig into his living room to try it out and now she is refusing to help put it back after his failure.

But this is a situation that might have to change moving forward. The next-gen Xbox machine, codenamed Helix has already been confirmed as being able to play PC games. In a recent interview with Jason Ronald, Xbox VP of Next Gen, this was again reiterated.

"We're very clear on the design goal: Helix is designed to be a console that is also capable of playing games from your PC," says Ronald. "It is not a PC that can also play console games."

This means it's going to have to support PC games, and that potentially means baked in support for keyboard and mouse in the hardware itself, rather than enabled on a per-title basis. After all, PC games kinda take those inputs for granted, no? So, maybe Red Dead Redemption 3 on Project Helix might come with keyboard and mouse support from the get-go, even if it's not necessarily released on PC straight away.

Still, for GTA 6 right now, basically it's controller or nothing, so make sure to get yourself a good pad—that's one of the biggest upgrades I've made to my setup for GTA 6.

#3695. Two Cool, Hidden Features GTA 6 Doesn’t Explain: Flipping And Sitting

Grand Theft Auto 6 is out now after a long wait, and as players invade Vice City like a swarm of hungry rats, they’re likely to poke at all its missions, tutorials, and random events. And yet, most of them likely won’t realize that hidden in GTA 6 and its massive amount of controls are two very cool and much-appreciated features: the ability to flip cars over and to sit on the ground and chill.

In past GTA games, flipping a car onto its back was a death sentence for the vehicle. It would soon catch on fire and blow up, which could be very annoying. Then in GTA V, Rockstar added the ability to flip your car over by rocking the left thumbstick around. While this was handy, it always felt like an out-of-place mechanic that was too convenient. It almost felt like magic and trivialized rolling a car over in a crash. With GTA 6, Rockstar has implemented an option that lets you salvage a stolen car that gets flipped on its back, without the use of magic.

Simply walk up against the side of the flipped vehicle and click the left stick in as either Jason or Lucia. If done correctly, the character should move their arms into position and start pushing on the car. At that point, you can hold square or X to attempt to flip the car back onto its wheels. If the vehicle is too heavy or you run out of stamina, the flip won’t work. I’ve also had it fail on steep inclines.

You can also push cars down the road if they run out of gas or shove a boat or jet ski off the sand and into the water using this mechanic. For most people, this won’t be a super-useful feature, as you can just use the Scooter Bros app to repair your car or respawn it for a fee. But if you’re out and about in a stolen car and being chased by the cops, which blocks access to the app, being able to flip a speedy getaway car back over could prove handy.

I’ve played over 140 hours of Grand Theft Auto 6 at this point, and I don’t remember the game, at any point in those many, many hours, explaining that I could do this. I only discovered it by accident when, after flipping a car over, I got close enough to it for a small tutorial prompt to appear in the top left, hinting at the ability. Later, I tried pushing a small boat off a trailer into the water, and it worked. Neat!

Another feature the game never really explained to me (or I missed) is the ability to sit or rest anywhere in the game.

Simply hold circle or B while on foot and your character will attempt to rest. In some areas, like on grass or sand, this will let Jason and Lucia sit and chill. In other places, they’ll lean on one foot and relax. And if you do this near a wall, they’ll rest against it like a cool person.

Again, this is a feature that I don’t remember the game explicitly explaining to me while playing. I discovered this early on when I tried to see if I could go prone and held the crouch button. I didn’t go prone, but I did pop a squat on the dirt.

I really love that GTA 6 added the ability to just…sit and chill out almost anywhere. The series has rarely let players relax and take in the world in this way. Sometimes I’d find a busy section of the beach in Vice City and sit on the sand, just watching the many different NPCs mill about. Other times I’d find a campfire in the woods and sit next to it in the dark, listening to the world around me. I hope you enjoy sitting and flipping as much as I do in GTA 6. Take a break between the shooting and the robbing. Jason and Lucia deserve it.

It’s a common practice for celebrity couples to keep their private lives, well private, and it’s no different for Zendaya and Tom Holland. While the two choose to keep things private, they understand the “parasocial investment” fans have in their relationship. However, even big-name directors can’t help sharing funny relationship stories about them, such as dishing about Holland’s funny reaction to seeing Zendaya in The Odyssey, and it’s just too perfect.

Director Christopher Nolan continued to praise Zendaya’s performance when he sat down with Stephen Spielberg during a special screening of The Odyssey. However, this time around he shared what her husband’s reaction was to seeing her play a goddess, and it’s probably not what you think. During the Q&A (via People) in West Hollywood, California, Nolan revealed there was a moment that got a little too real for Holland:

Vice City has changed a lot over the years - but maybe less than you think

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

With GTA 6 now so tantalizingly close that it's in the hands of players willing and able to pull off the New Zealand trick, it's very easy to get caught up in the now. After a 13-year wait for GTA 6, it can be easy to forget that all of the other GTA games were made over the span of just 12 years. But that's not what happened at Rockstar, as Stuart Petri, VP of art for 2D/UI design lays out - instead, he says that GTA 6 was the result of an uninterrrupted, 25-year process.

In Rockstar's development notes, shared with press ahead of the GTA 6 review drop, Petri notes that "almost 25 years ago, we helped bring Vice City to life." That first foray to Rockstar's take on Florida "began as a simple visual design language," but has since "evolved into something far more sophisticated, layered, and considered."

As Rockstar returns to Vice City for the first time since 2006's Vice City Stories, Petri notes that "we're returning to a world that has grown enormously in detail, creativity, and gameplay complexity." That meant that the series' art had to change too, ensuring it was relevant to a modern audience while "retaining the heritage that makes it unmistakably GTA."

Petri discusses plenty about the discipline of UI art, but it's the underlying message about the history of Grand Theft Auto and the wider GTA identity that I think is most interesting. This series feels like such a known quantity, but it's really not - the world has changed an awful lot since 2013, and that's before we even touch on the differences in the gaming industry. Rockstar is releasing this game into a landscape that's wildly different to the one they last launched a Grand Theft Auto game into, but that doesn't seem to have phased Petri at all. In his part of the game, he says, "it's about building on that heritage" that the series thrives on, "and creating something that feels both entirely new and, at the same time, unmistakably GTA." He finishes by saying that "25 years on, the DNA remains," tying the very first version of Vice City to the one that we're all about to experience.

#3691. All 34 of the infamously fired Rockstar staff appear in GTA 6 game credits, though some aren't listed as "former employees", curiously

UPDATE: The final few names have been confirmed.

UPDATE 19TH NOVEMBER: All of the 34 fired Rockstar employees appear in the credits for GTA 6. We were able to confirm the final few names' existence there after Rockstar posted the full credits online - in searchable form. Before this, the process of cross-checking was intensely laborious: it required watching a scrolling list of names for an hour-and-a-half to see if they appeared.

Also, we couldn't identify six names in the "former employees" section of the credits before because they don't appear there, we now know. These names appear listed under the departments the people worked for, as if they still worked at Rockstar. Why this is, we don't know - perhaps it's something to do with being involved in the employment tribunal or not. We're asking Rockstar for clarification.

ORIGINAL STORY 18TH NOVEMBER: Eurogamer can confirm that at least 28 of the 34 employees fired by Rockstar roughly a year ago - in an action that directly led to the employment tribunal Rockstar is currently facing in Scotland - are named in the credits of Grand Theft Auto 6.

A number of those fired employees are seeking compensation for unfair dismissal amid allegations of "union busting", in an employment tribunal that comes to an end today. The delayed climax of the case couldn't be more fateful, aligned as it is with tomorrow's release of GTA 6, and the outcome will be historic either way.

Rockstar recently revealed that more than 4,711 people worked at the company making GTA 6, employed across 12 offices around the world - a staff-count that has more than doubled since Red Dead Redemption 2. It's a game that's wowed critics - Eurogamer awarded GTA 6 five stars in our review this afternoon - and which observers expect to generate $2bn in revenue in its opening weekend alone.

But perhaps Christian Donlan put it best when digesting the opulence on display in the Netflix 'extended look' GTA 6 trailer. "To spend all this money making something so beautifully rich and detailed, to pay billions for this game and sweat every little animation, to float it out to us on Netflix, amongst genuine discussion around whether Netflix can handle it? That's commitment," he wrote. "And if you're willing to do that, and willing to do that to tell an underdog story, you should let your workers who made everything form a union."

The aim-assisting PureVector technology in this mouse promises a lot, but in my case it fails to deliver, as my aim doesn't improve from turning it on. It's a solid, lightweight, competitive mouse regardless, but it's too expensive for what it is without delivering the PureVector promise.

PC Gamer's got your back Our experienced team dedicates many hours to every review, to really get to the heart of what matters most to you. Find out more about how we evaluate games and hardware.

Corsair is continuing the 2026 trend of brands pushing out new and innovative mouse technologies. In this case, it's all in the 'PureVector' part of the name. In partnership with AimLabs, Corsair has made a mouse that can adjust sensitivity in different directions to tailor it to your movements and help you aim better.

That's the claim, anyway. In practice, I've found that PureVector hasn't improved my aim, both subjectively while gaming and objectively based on multiple AimLabs tests. Some pro players that Corsair highlights claim it's helped them, so your mileage may vary.

Apart from PureVector, though, the mouse itself deserves some attention, as it's still a very performant, lightweight mouse for competitive gaming. It has some upgrades compared to its predecessor, the Sabre V2 Pro, too.

✅ You want to try the latest tech: You might get better results than I did with PureVector. It tailors sensor sensitivity in different directions based on how you aim.

❌ You want good value for the basics: If you just want a comfy mouse with solid build quality that performs well, you can find something of better value elsewhere.

The aim-assisting PureVector technology in this mouse promises a lot, but in my case it fails to deliver, as my aim doesn't improve from turning it on. It's a solid, lightweight, competitive mouse regardless, but it's too expensive for what it is without delivering on the PureVector promise.

Replacement skates, USB-A to USB-C cable, wireless dongle, AimLabs PureVector software integration

In most ways, the Sabre V3 Pro PureVector Ergo is your standard competitive gaming mouse: lightweight, few frills, simple design, good sensor. It is lighter than most competitive mice with a solid shell, though a little heavier than its predecessor, the Sabre V2 Pro.

Setting aside the PureVector aiming shenanigans for a moment, probably the biggest improvement compared to the Sabre V2 Pro is its battery life, which has been doubled. Apart from that, you're getting a 42,000 DPI sensor, optical clicks, and some bigger replacement skates included in the box.

Now we come to the main attraction: PureVector. Corsair has designed the mouse's internals and firmware to permit different sensitivities in different directions. So, for instance, it can move slightly slower horizontally than vertically.

Corsair has worked with AimLabs to let you test your aiming in the latter software and then have the mouse adjust your directional sensitivity for you. The PureVector software within AimLabs has been made with the help of a bunch of aiming data (over 4 billion data points, apparently) and machine learning. The end result is, in theory, a mouse that can tailor its sensitivity in different directions to stop you over-shooting or under-shooting your target.

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

Again, in theory, this should also save you time when you aim, and Corsair claims it can save more time than reducing the latency of clicks—the latter is, for example, what we see the Logitech G Pro X2 Superstrike and X3 Superstrike focusing on.

It's worth noting that Corsair highlights a number of pro players who say they've benefitted from this new tech. However, for my part, I haven't noticed a difference.

For reference, I play Counter-Strike 2 at about FaceIt Level 7 or Premier 18–20,000 rating (approx. top 25%). I'm far from a pro, but I'm far from the worst. In-game, I didn't notice any difference between my aim with PureVector set up and with it disabled.

I also repeatedly tested my aim in the AimLabs SpiderShot Precision test, and I actually had slightly better results using another mouse without PureVector (the SteelSeries Sensei Pro), and the latter mouse my hand was less familiar with.

More than this, though, I can't help but feel that it's a bit of a band-aid solution to poor aim. If you're overshooting your shots when you aim left, for instance, you could get PureVector to lower your sensitivity in that direction. But why not instead work on training your hand not to overshoot? That way, having good aim won't be dependent on using this one mouse, and you can get used to aiming consistently in different directions.

PureVector aside, the Sabre V3 Pro performs well. The sensor is great and feels very responsive. Ditto the new optical mouse clicks. I have no complaints about its performance as a general mouse, I just don't see the use in PureVector myself. Of course, your mileage may vary, as it seems to have for some pro players.

One area where the Sabre V3 Pro does particularly shine, just like the Sabre V2 Pro, is in its light weight. This latest iteration feels even sturdier than the previous one and still manages to be lighter than most competitive gaming mice.

Battery life is a definite selling point of the Sabre V3 Pro PureVector. It's a lot better than I was expecting. The Sabre V2 Pro can only manage about 70 hours at 1 kHz, and this new one doubles that to 140 hours.

I think Corsair has struck a great balance here, because it's not as light as the V2—which was 36 g—but 41 g is still incredibly light, and I'd much rather have the bigger battery than shave off those few extra grams. You're not getting any fancy wireless charging or hot-swappable batteries here, but 140 hours of battery life is great.

The Corsair Sabre V3 Pro PureVector Ergo is, as its excruciatingly long name suggests, pretty ergonomic. It's not the biggest ergo mouse I've used—the Zowie EC2-DW and SteelSeries Rival Pro both feel a bit bigger in-hand—but it still feels comfy under my medium-sized palm.

There's also a non-ergo, symmetrical version for the same price, and you can get carbon fiber or magnesium versions for each, if you're willing to spend even more ($200 and $230, respectively).

I like the lightweight ergonomic version, though. Its slightly smaller size, combined with its light weight, also means holding it in a fingertip or claw grip doesn't feel too bad, which isn't something you can say about many ergonomic mice. Palm grip is still the main intention here, though. Playing Counter-Strike on low sensitivity feels great.

Build quality is decent, too, which is a bit of a relief because the previous version, the Sabre V2 Pro, sacrificed some on this front to achieve its 'ultralight' status. There's no creak or flex along the sides, and only a slight bit of flex on the underside. The side buttons feel great, with no pre-travel, and the scroll wheel has well-defined steps.

There is some pre-travel to the left- and right-mouse buttons, however, and they don't feel as satisfying to press as some other mice like the Razer Viper V4 Pro or SteelSeries Rival Pro. They're far from bad, just not quite up to the standard of some other expensive gaming mice I've tried.

The version I've got here, the 'Ergo' one, is pretty plain and looks quite similar to its predecessor, the Sabre V2 Pro. It's plain white, with only some very subtle grey accents. I'm fine with that, as the focus is on performance and comfort.

Any extra aesthetic fancies are likely to add to the weight, which isn't worth the sacrifice for this kind of mouse. As with most ultralight mice, you know what you're getting aesthetically, and it's minimal.

This mouse uses the same software as the previous V2 Pro. What's noteworthy is the software is browser-based—there's no locally-installable app to use. That's mainly because you're expected to just set it and go, without returning to adjust things.

You can set up profiles to toggle between DPI using a mouse button combination, however. And the web software can be used offline if you install it as an app in your browser, so internet outages shouldn't cause any problems.

The web hub is basic but gets the job done. The battery indicator isn't very precise, only showing a tiny icon and no percentage numbers, but that's my only complaint.

The AimLabs integration is perfectly fine, too. Assuming you've got it installed on Steam, you can allow the web hub to boot it up for you from there, or boot it up yourself. Once in, you can navigate to PureVector and let it run you through the aim training to adjust your sensitivity in different sweep directions. It's intuitive, and the directional charts it shows are clear enough.

At $180/£160, the Sabre V3 Pro PureVector Ergo is an expensive mouse. It joins the likes of the G Pro X2/X3 Superstrike, Viper V4 Pro, DeathAdder V4 Pro, SteelSeries Rival Pro, and other high-end, competitive gaming mice.

Can it compete with these? In my opinion, not quite. These other gaming mice each have extra features and new technologies that go some way towards justifying the very high price tags. The Superstrikes have analogue clicks, the Viper V4 Pro has FrameSync, the Rival Pro has hot-swappable batteries and UWB connectivity.

The DeathAdder V4 Pro doesn't have anything too fancy like that, but is a very solid gaming mouse. I'd class the Sabre V3 Pro PureVector in this category, alongside the DeathAdder. That's because while the PureVector technology is indeed very new, I haven't found it to have much of an impact, and so I'm left considering its merits as a general competitive gaming mouse, setting aside this new aim assist tech.

There are merits to it that justify a price tag above $100: light weight, comfy ergonomic shape, optical clicks, responsive scroll wheel, great battery life. But not enough to justify $180—not without something extra, which PureVector promises but, in my case, fails to deliver. Unless, that is, you're set on getting a mouse as light as this one is that still has a sturdy shell.

You could instead, for instance, go for something like the Mchose K7 V2 Ultra+ for about $90. Or a Pulsar mouse like the Pulsar X2 CrazyLight for $130, which sometimes drops to about $100 on sale.

If you fancy spending the extra to try it out for yourself and see if you can get the kinds of benefits the pros that Corsair highlights espouse, go for it. But for my money, I'd be opting for a cheaper lightweight mouse, or one with better build quality like the Viper V4 Pro.

#3689. PSA: Some GTA 6 Ultimate Edition content is only available for the first chapter, and you'll have to put in hard graft to unlock more

GTA 6's Ultimate Edition has proven enormously popular, despite its hefty $100 price tag. So much so that Strauss Zelnick, boss of Rockstar parent company Take-Two, recently confirmed it's the edition most people are buying - and that's despite a lack of specific information about how its unlockable content works. With GTA 6 just hours away from release, however - and out now in certain parts of the work - details are beginning to emerge, and the answer is perhaps a little surprising.

As previously confirmed, the $100/£90 Ultimate Edition provides access to exclusive vehicles, weapons, shops, and more, with the full list as follows:

Rockstar also previously revealed that "Ultimate Edition bonuses become available to Jason and Lucia across their story, with new items uncovered behind each chapter". The specifics of how - and when - all this stuff unlocks, though, remained unclear. So if you've opted for the Ultimate Edition, you might be wondering where your stuff is when you finally fire up the game. As reported by IGN, which has full unlock details, it turns out virtually all of GTA 6's Ultimate Edition content, as per details in the in-game shop, requires progressing through the main story - in some cases dozens and dozens of hours into the story - before it'll become available.

Ultimate Edition-exclusive shops, for instance, unlock during Chapter 1, and many of the other additions become available by the end of Chapter 2. That doesn't sound too difficult, but as Eurogamer's Chris Tapsell notes, reaching that point could take upward of 25 hours. As for some of the late-game unlocks, such as the Shitzu Squalo and the Vice City Style outfits and tattoos (available in Chapter 4) and Chapter 5's 95 Grotti Cheetah, you could be looking at closing in on 60 hours of playtime before they unlock.

"It'll vary depending how hard people focus on the main story," Chris explains, "but if you were mostly focused on the main story plus the optional character-based missions in largely chronological order, that's about how long it'd take."

It's also worth noting - perhaps surprisingly - that some Ultimate Edition content is only a temporary unlock, usable only during specific chapters. Jason's Dinka Enduro motorcycle and Crest Kayak, for instance, can only be accessed and enjoyed during Chapter 1. That's also true for his retro Vapid Ganado, available from the Coastal Auto Care mod shop in Key Lento. So basically, you'll want to make the most of these while you can!

All this might be a little disappointing for players who were expecting to be showered with Ultimate Edition spoils from the off (and that they'd be permanent unlocks), but the good news is 60 hours in GTA 6 is far from a chore. As Chris explained in his five star GTA 6 review, Rockstar's latest is an "irreducible mix of silliness, intimacy, grand ideas and rock 'n' roll action" that "pushes back the horizon of video games once again".

As a child of the early 2000s, I grew up obsessed with Gilmore Girls and Gossip Girl. These remarkable teen shows were irresistible, and they are how I was introduced to Jared Padalecki and Leighton Meester. So, you can imagine my excitement when I learned that these actors would be leading the rom-com, Guarding Stars, on the 2026 Christmas movie schedule together. So, I had to ask about how they bonded over their time on shows like Gilmore Girls and Gossip Girl, and Padalecki’s G-oriented response hilariously surprised me.

When I brought all this up to Jared Padalecki, who plays actor Jack Stapleton in Guarding Stars, he said he did speak to Meester about their time on The CW and their work on the “G-titled girl shows,” as Padalecki affectionately called them. Elaborating on that hilarious point, the Supernatural star said:

Yeah, we did talk about it here and there. We didn't get into deep, deep detail. But yeah, I also joke that I was in Gilmore Girls; she was in Gossip Girl. Then there's Golden Girls. We were all on the double G titled girl shows. Well, I didn't get to be on Golden Girls, but I wish.

Well, I certainly didn’t see this hilarious point coming. While I’ve always been entertained by the fact that both Jared Padalecki and Leighton Meester were on maybe two of the three most famous [insert name that starts with G] Girl(s) shows around, I didn’t think he’d bring it up. I also didn’t think he’d say he wanted to be on Golden Girls, but now I wish that could have happened somehow.

Anyway, getting back to the Gossip Girl and Gilmore Girls vets working together, Padalecki said their similar experiences of getting their break on major television programs did help them bond on set. In fact, as they filmed Guarding Stars, which is a Christmas flick on the 2026 movie schedule, in the cold, they found themselves discussing how the industry has evolved with some of their other co-stars:

But we did talk about it and just how the industry in general has changed. Especially, there'd be scenes where it was too cold to wait outside in between takes, so they'd have a warming hut for us or a warming room, and having Andie MacDowell there to talk about when she had started and the differences and this and that, and so we would bond about it.

Yeah, this book-to-screen adaptation of Katherine Center’s The Bodyguard is full of veteran actors. I can only imagine the conversations Padalecki, Meester and MacDowell, who plays Padalecki’s mom in the movie, had. Speaking more to that point, the actor told me that he and the Gossip Girl star's similar TV history did really help them work together:

But I think there was just more than talking about it. There was just an understanding when we got to set that she's a technician and she's talented, and she's done hundreds of hours of work. And I think hopefully she thought the same me, so we just hit the ground running. It wasn't like, ‘No, here's how you hit a mark, and here's how you find the lens.’ Like, I knew she knew; she knew I knew. It's like, ‘Cool, let's play. Let's see what the words bring us.’

So, the double-G connection, if you will, really served them well on this. While Meester and Padalecki were never on the same shows, they both broke big through projects that aired on The CW, and having that background helped them get off to a great start in Guarding Stars.

Now, in this new G project the two actors star in, Padalecki plays an actor, and Meester is his bodyguard. However, to maintain their cover with his parents, they have to fake date. It’s a very fun, wholesome, and action-packed movie that’s well worth the time. And if you’re a fan of the “double G-titled girl shows,” you really won’t want to miss it.

With that said, Guarding Stars is available to stream with a Netflix subscription. And if you’d like to stream “the double G-titled girl shows,” you can catch Gilmore Girls and Golden Girls with either a Disney+ or Hulu subscription, and Gossip Girl is streaming for those with an HBO Max subscription.

#3687. Even the PS5 Pro is "not powerful enough" to run GTA 6 at 60FPS or 40FPS, Rockstar says

Don't expect GTA 6 to get an update supporting higher framerate modes, at least, not on current-generation consoles. Rockstar has explained that even the most powerful console of the bunch, the PS5 Pro, isn't powerful enough to run the lavish game at 40FPS or 60FPS.

Last week, some players weren't too happy with the news that GTA 6 is targeting 30FPS on all platforms it's currently launching on - PS5 Pro, PS5, Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S. Like countless other big productions this generation, the hope was that Rockstar Games would offer both quality and performance modes for its lush open-world monster.

Rockstar's now seemingly confirmed that its crime epic won't run at 60FPS or 40FPS anytime soon, simply because it can't on the currently available hardware.

"While the PS5 Pro's central processor is slightly better than the PS5 base console, it is not powerful enough to run the game's complex simulation at higher frame rates," the studio's technology production director, Marc Chambers, said in a statement to Kotaku. There you have it, then - even the beefiest console around can't handle Leonida at higher framerates.

Chambers did note some of the souped up console's other technical improvements, however: "Our base presentation makes use of ray-traced reflections and global illumination. On the PS5 Pro, this is enhanced with the addition of ray-traced shadows, as well as overall added clarity through the use of PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR). The PS5 Pro features an upgraded graphics processor and upscaling technology that we leverage to increase the game's visual fidelity."

The tech gurus over at Digital Foundry gave some more insight into how GTA 6 runs on current-gen machines, calling it a "technical tour de force," though one that can still dip below 30FPS on PS5 and Xbox Series X during busier chase scenes and explosive shootouts. It's perhaps unsurprising, then, that higher framerates are off the table for now.

A 30FPS launch is by no means a departure for Rockstar Games, either. GTA 5 also ran at an unsteady 30FPS when it first dropped onto the Xbox 360 and PS3, with 60FPS support only coming alongside the game's PC port more than a year later. I'm not too fussed about the game's 30FPS target, personally. I'd much rather have a game that consistently hits 30FPS than one that continuously chugs trying to reach 60FPS, especially when it's as frequently drop dead gorgeous as GTA 6.

The slightly lower framerates haven't affected the game's critical response so far, either. In Eurogamer's GTA 6 review, our Chris Tapsell called it a "game of opposites and awe, minute detail and impossible scale" as "Rockstar pushes back the horizon of video games once again."

If you're planning to jump into the game at midnight - or if you're virtually travelling to New Zealand for early entry - there's a few things to be aware of. First is that you won't be able to replay GTA 6's missions without multiple save files, so be sure to soak it all up. Second, some Ultimate Edition content is only available in the first chapter.

GTA 6 is finally here, and some players have been surprised to find themselves spending more time running errands and doing home repair than, you know, stealing cars through the game's opening hours. Rockstar was absolutely devoted to spending that vast development budget simulating the minutiae of Jason and Lucia's lives, and it's all pretty reminiscent of another infamously expensive game: Sega's Shenmue.

Shenmue made headlines back in 1999 as the most expensive game ever made, with a reported $70 million budget – that'd be about $140 million, accounting for inflation. That number has, of course, been eclipsed multiple times over through the past few decades, but it's still pretty expensive, especially in a world where AAA-beating GOTY contenders like Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 are being made for less than $10 million.

We still don't know Rockstar's actual budget for GTA 6, but it's tough to imagine it's anything less than the new most expensive game ever made. There is, of course, a key difference between Grand Theft Auto and Shenmue: Sega's game was not financially successful, failing to recoup its development costs.

Yet Shenmue developed a cult following thanks to its obvious ambition. It was promoted as the first part of a multi-game martial arts epic, which would see protagonist Ryo Hazuki on a globe-trotting quest for revenge. But fighting makes up only a tiny part of the game. You instead spend much of your time exploring a small but densely packed open world, living out Ryo's day-to-day life as you rummage through drawers, drive forklifts, and question wandering NPCs for clues to your next objective.

The early hours of GTA 6 offer a lot more possibility for high-octane chaos, but the game gently encourages you to instead spend your time restoring your home, running errands for neighbors, working out, eating meals, and chatting up random NPCs. In a way, it feels like the fulfillment of Shenmue's ambition – the life simulation now offers genuine payoffs instead of the charming jank we got in 1999.

You'll find this sort of comparison coming up again and again among retro gaming sickos on social media. "Gta 6 is not for the 'normals'," Twitter user drag writes. ""it's for real gamers who spent hours on shenmue buying toy capsules of sonic, it's 89.99 deadly premonition."

"Played a couple hours into GTA6 and um… Yeah, it's a Shenmue game," Alex Lemley says on Bluesky. "They made a Shenmue game, actually. It's a really good Shenmue game, but it's Shenmue."

#3685. GTA 6 won't let you use cheats until you complete the main story, and locks progression when you do

Here's a twist: you can't use cheats in Grand Theft Auto 6 until you complete the entire game's main story.

That's what we discovered from our tests at least, after loading in saves at various points through the game to be sure, and it's also both a first for the series and a departure even from how developer Rockstar handled cheats in Red Dead Redemption 2. In that game,approximately half of the cheats were available from the off, and the other half required discovering specific newspapers from around the game's world to unlock.

In GTA 6, you'll again need to do some legwork. This time it appears that all of the game's cheats not only require you to finish the story, but also complete various tasks or challenges to unlock them.

The way it works is simple enough. Once you finish the main story, the "Cheats" tab - previously hidden - quietly appears at the far end of the Progress menu, accessible when you open the in-game map and scroll with the bumper buttons. From there, you can view various sub-sections of cheats, sorted by category, and a list of 10 or so cheats for each.

With each cheat there'll be a short explanation of what it does, and what's required to unlock it and, once unlocked, guidance on how to perform it. This is done via whipping out your phone, holding down the shoulder buttons and using various D-Pad inputs - much the same as GTA 5.

There's also another caveat to bear in mind: when you use a cheat, you'll see a notification warning you that the game can't be saved while it's active, and that Trophies and Achievements are also disabled until you end that session. This makes sense, once you understand the nature of GTA 6's story - there is a cheat for giving yourself a load of money, for instance; another departure from GTA 5 where that popular cheat was removed - but given you'll need certain amounts of cash at various points of the story, enabling you to shortcut that would disrupt the way the narrative unfolds.

We'll have a guide from yours truly to all the game's cheats live on Eurogamer in the very near future, as the game releases here in the UK. In the meantime, if you find yourself on the fence about this one, be sure to give our GTA 6 review a look. As I put it there, giving the game five stars: it is "the most believable and unbelievable video game world ever made".

I just found a curious artifact of the Old West in GTA 6, and the best part is I stumbled across it completely by accident.

That's right, partner: Arthur Morgan's cowboy hat is in Grand Theft Auto 6, and you won't find it in some trendy Western fashion shop or in a McMansion as part of a wealthy crypto bro's collection.

If you want to wear it yourself, I'll tell you below where you can find it.

I was out in Port Gellhorn looking for a particular kind of car for reasons completely unrelated to clothing accessories. While I was driving, I spotted a sign on the side of the road with a balloon tied to it, reading "Yard Sale" with an arrow pointing down the road.

I followed the sign which led to more yard sale signs and, yup, sure enough, the signs pointed me to an actual yard sale. And among the items for sale was a very familiar-looking hat.

It's called a "Genuine Cowboy Hat" and, this being a yard sale, it only cost $5. But I knew the second I saw it that this was no ordinary cowboy hat. Here, have a look at it from the back.

Yep. No mistaking that. I even got a little pang of sadness thinking about good ol' Arthur Morgan. I miss him. Maybe when I'm done with GTA 6, I'll strap on my spurs and take another ride through Red Dead Redemption 2.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Directions: Head to Port Gellhorn. It's in Kelly County on the western side of the state along the coast. In the southern tip of Port Gellhorn, there's a small neighborhood of about five houses just northwest of the Dirt Merchants mod shop.

Look for the driveway filled with yard sale clutter: furniture and electronics and such. There's a bunch of balloons, a cut-out of a nearly naked cowboy, and a big American flag flying. You'll find the hat toward the back sitting on top of a guitar case on a couch. There's also a shirt, a cap, and some shoes for sale that definitely didn't belong to Arthur.

#3683. Delete GTA 6 from your hard drive and indie publisher Devolver Digital might give you a free game

GTA 6 is out at midnight everywhere (19th November), but it's far from the only game in town. Indie publisher Devolver Digital is taking on the open-world behemoth with its very own Volvy's Adventure: Reslimed, out the same day, and you can win a free copy of the platformer by proving you've deleted GTA 6 off your hard drive.

"Want a free copy of November's hottest release? Repost this tweet with a video of you deleting your GTA6 pre-load along with #MakeRoomForVolvy for a chance to win a copy of Volvy's Adventure: Reslimed on Steam," the publisher wrote on social media.

It's not every day you see a publisher promote its own games by asking folks to delete another company's release, but arguably the wildest part of the giveaway is that Volvy's Adventure isn't launching on consoles. Even if you were to scrub GTA 6's 212GB pre-load from your PS5 or Xbox, you're definitely not making room for Volvy.

"Heads up: Volvy's Adventure: Reslimed is launching exclusively on PC. While we expect to see console GTA deletions in your submissions, Steam keys are the only prize available for this giveaway," Devolver noted.

Devolver made quite an amusing GTA 6 parody trailer, as well, which sees Volvy and Miss Volvy running from the police and getting steamy in the shower. I've embedded it up above for your viewing pleasure.

For the unaware, Volvy used to be a common fixture at Devolver Digital's frequently bonkers notE3 presentations. He's now somewhat of a company mascot. But while Volvy's Adventure: Reslimed is being presented as a "much-anticipated remaster of the original remake of the hit action-platformer," this is, in fact, Volvy's first proper game. Making up an elaborate history for Volvy is just part of the publisher's long-running and increasingly questionable gag.

Gunbrella and Gato Robot developer doinksoft is behind this one, a throwback side-scrolling platformer where our mouse-like mascot uses his oversized hand to helicopter over gaps, punch through roadblocks and, erm, fist himself underground, per the game's Steam page.

Devolver Digital has been waiting to steal Rockstar's thunder for well over a year now. The publisher threatened to release a game on GTA 6's release date way back in May 2025, and has pushed back its plan with each new GTA 6 delay. Gotta respect the commitment, at least.

Ebenzer was at the top of the box office when it arrived in theaters, but the book to screen adaptation didn't make that much money compared to Depp's past projects. Over on the Naughty But Nice Substack, writer Rob Shuter quoted an alleged industry insider, who spoke about how the movie's performance may influence the future of Johnny Depp's career. In their words:

This was Johnny’s test, and he got a C. That’s not good enough for a studio looking to spend a fortune on a franchise. The problem is, it wasn’t a complete disaster. If the movie had totally bombed, everyone could walk away and move on. Instead, these middle-of-the-road numbers leave Hollywood with a difficult decision.

At the time of writing this story, Ebenzer has made $43.4 million on a reported budget of $38 million. Johnny Depp took a huge pay cut to keep at number low, but it wasn't enough to reach huge box office numbers of previous projects like the Pirates of the Caribbean movies. If this source is to be believed, the powers at Hollywood might not be inclined to give him major gigs following how Ti West's new movie did.

Ebenezer's cast has plenty of familiar faces, but Depp has been front and center of the movie's promotional tour. He even showed up at San Diego Comic-Con dressed as Scrooge. Fans have been wondering if the actor might return as Captain Jack Sparrow in another Pirates movie, but according to the same source, that might be less likely after Ebenezer. They claimed:

Pirates is the ultimate prize for Johnny, but Hollywood needs to know audiences still want to see him. Nostalgia alone won’t sell hundreds of millions of dollars in tickets.

We should probably take these quotes with a grain of salt, but it should be interesting to see where/if Johnny Depp appears in another major film production. He returned to acting in Jeanne du Barry, but that was a French film produced outside of the Hollywood machine. While he's got plenty of beloved movies on his resume, it's unclear if moviegoing audiences can get past the Amber Heard ordeal and still want to show up in theaters to see him on the big screen.

Ebenezer is in theaters now as part of the 2026 movie release list. We'll have to see how much money it makes deeper into its theatrical run, as well as what projects Johnny Depp signs on for next.

GTA 6 is slowly rolling out across the globe. The crime epic's already available to play in countries such as South Korea and New Zealand, but Japanese players are finding out that male nudity is only partially obscured by a thin black thong that covers Jason and the other men in Leonida.

Last week, we reported that GTA 6 might have been censored in Japan since the region's age rating board lacked any mention of the "sexual content" we knew it would include elsewhere. The Japanese version's install size was also notably smaller than other places in the world.

Now that GTA 6 is finally in the hands of players, we have a better idea of what was left out and/or covered up in Japan. Multiple social media accounts playing the game in Japan have reported that when you take main man Jason into the shower, his butt is only kinda covered up by a thong. GTA 6 is far from the only game that's dealt with regional censorship in Japan, however. Baldur's Gate 3 and The Witcher 3 had their most salacious scenes censored in some manner, for example. And even GTA 5 had to remove its infamous torture scene for approval in Japan. It's quite possible GTA 6 has had to cover more than just the backside of nude men to go on sale in the country, although those regional differences won't become entirely clear until players get further through the story.

If you're one of the countless millions contributing to the collective endangering of global productivity by enjoying Grand Theft Auto 6 at launch, you might have paused in the middle of blatantly disregarding traffic laws to wonder: Wait a second, am I hearing "Weird Al" Yankovic hosting this pretend radio station?

And yes, you are: In a Bluesky post earlier today, the beloved comedic musician and polka maestro confirmed that he offered his voice for DJ Al, who hosts '80s music station Vice City FM alongside Swedish actress, model, and singer Brigitte Nielsen. Their contributions were then double-confirmed by the full GTA 6 credits, which Rockstar published once launch time hit.

I’m the host of GTA 6’s “non-stop ‘80s” radio channel Vice City FM. I also wrote some in-game commercials, and I’m the voice of the Burger Shot ads as well! As a long-time fan of the Grand Theft Auto franchise, I couldn’t be more excited about this. Okay, gotta get back to playing the game!

"I’m the host of GTA 6’s 'non-stop ‘80s' radio channel Vice City FM. I also wrote some in-game commercials, and I’m the voice of the Burger Shot ads as well!" Yankovic said. "As a long-time fan of the Grand Theft Auto franchise, I couldn’t be more excited about this. Okay, gotta get back to playing the game!"

Somewhere out there, Weird Al is securing the love of his virtual latina wife, and I think that's beautiful.

Yankovic is just one of countless recognizable names you'll find if you scroll down the GTA 6 credits. Among the core cast, SNL alumnus Bobby Moynihan voices Cal, Jason's bumbling, conspiracy-brained buddy. The pair's criminal boss man, Brian Heder, is performed by legendary Stephen Root—who you'll likely recognize as Bill Dauterive on King of the Hill, Milton in Office Space, and all kinds of magnificent weirdos across the Coen brothers filmography.

But it's the radio talent where GTA 6's credits get particularly wild. It's a cavalcade of international music icons, comedians, and film figures. While driving around GTA 6, you might hear Lana Del Rey hosting Back Country Radio, or Latin music phenom Bad Bunny on Cocoteo FM. On Dirty South Classics, there's Trina, Trick Daddy, and Gucci Mane. Pop station Flash FM is helmed by Robyn and Alex Consani—the first transgender model to win Model of the Year at the British Fashion Awards and celebrated TikTok goofball. Keith Richards is in there. I didn't even know he was still capable of speech.

On talk radio, you can hear Ted Lasso's Jason Sudeikis, Abbot Elementary's Janelle James, and John Leguizamo of being John Leguizamo fame. Stavros Halkias is on there doing a Conservative talk radio bit. But maybe the most compelling inclusion, for me, is that Kaleidoscope FM is hosted by Jeremy Irons. The Academy Award-winning actor. You were in Kafka, Jeremy. How'd you end up in cyber-Florida?

#3678. It really seems like Xbox isn't allowed to say GTA 6 at all

Like many major brands, Xbox is finding all sorts of ways to associate with the biggest game launch of the year: Grand Theft Auto 6. Unlike indie publisher Devolver Digital, however, Xbox has cleverly avoided ever mentioning GTA 6 directly in its marketing campaigns for GTA 6.

As pointed out by multiple people on social media, the Xbox Wire post titled 'How to Get Ready for November 19' is one all about celebrating the big release day of GTA 6, and helping players find ways to maximise their time with their Xbox consoles. Despite that, it does not mention GTA 6 by name a single time.

"Birthdays, anniversaries, and holidays have come and gone, but this day belongs to you and your Xbox console," the post reads, stopping short of saying why the day is important. "We can hardly believe it's almost here, either."

One day prior, Xbox Wire partnered with DJ Khaled to create custom doctor's notes for players to submit to their employers to take the day off. Why would you want to take 19th November off? Because you're apparently having "a serious case of Vitamin G deficiency".

Going even further back, Xbox revealed a custom-made Series X console it called X-Bite, which is a large, sculpted alligator that swallowed a Series X console. Why? Because "this November, Xbox is heading to Florida - home to incredible wildlife, unforgettable places, and every now and then, stories you have to see to believe."

Florida, of course, is the real-world US state GTA 6's Leonida is based on, but in keeping with the theme of not referring to the game - or its made-up state - directly, the blog does not.

Now, Xbox has directly named GTA 6 in places, but only when, seemingly, the post is about factual information. This Xbox Wire post reiterates GTA 6's Xbox Cloud streaming availability, and this one is a look-ahead at games launching the following week on Xbox. But that's about the extent of what you can expect.

So what's going on here? The simple guess is that PlayStation has a co-marketing deal with Rockstar, meaning no other console platform gets to use GTA 6's name in marketing. Sony is allowed to make custom, GTA 6-themed consoles, branded, limited-edition DualSense controllers and blaster the game all over the PS Blog, social media, and even change the PS App's icon colour to match the hue of GTA 6's.

This is all too similar to when, each year, various brands encourage you to buy their products to be ready for The Big Game, which is very distinct from the Super Bowl happening on the same day. Like Xbox, those brands simply don't have the rights to the real thing.

GTA 6 is available now on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S. In Eurogamer's five-star review, Chris Tapsell wrote, "Rockstar pushes back the horizon of video games once again with GTA 6. An irreducible mix of silliness, intimacy, grand ideas and rock 'n' roll action - and a load more after that."

Another married 90 Day Fiancé couple has broken up after marriage, as Rebecca Parrott recently announced that she and Zied Hakimi are no longer living together. The Last Resort was introduced as a couples' therapy retreat for 90 Day participants struggling in marriage. With the latest news from Rebecca on TikTok Live (via KikiandKibbitz), I think it's time to acknowledge the show's failings and how it may be doing more harm than good.

Rebecca and Zied's breakup isn't an isolated split for this particular show, as other couples called it quits on 90 Day: The Last Resort Season 3. Originally, I thought this might be the most breakups in a single season of the spinoff. However, I went down the list of every couple and discovered something pretty wild. Take a look:

Only three couples that have participated in 90 Day: Hunt For Love are currently confirmed to be still together. That's a pretty damning statistic for the therapists on this show, who have faced a lot of scrutiny for their advice to couples.

The 2026 TV schedule is just around the corner, and as the new year looms, there's already word that a new season is on the way. 90 Day insider @Shabooty shared a reported cast list for all the couples that will participate, but I'd be rethinking my decision after seeing the breakdown.

90 Day: The Last Resort could benefit from providing actual couples therapy for its participants, rather than a resort vacation that allows them to drink. We've seen couples therapy shows before on reality TV, and they work well. My question is why 90 Day Fiancé doesn't seem interested in that, nor do the participating couples.

Are 90 Day Fiancé: The Other Way’s Niles And Matilda Still Together After Ghana News? Here’s What We Know

I also think the audience would enjoy seeing that and would appreciate more success stories than we're currently seeing.

If 90 Day Fiancé is content to keep The Last Resort as it is, I would avoid that spinoff like the plague if I were invited. Of course, as a viewer, I'll continue to watch and enjoy episodes and hope that future couples have more success.

For a bunch of performance snobs, we are a surprisingly forgiving bunch at PC Gamer. Yes, if you try to insult XCOM, you're going to get a slap, but we've only just started playing GTA 6 (well, some of us) and we're mostly over the whole 'only runs at 30 fps' thing already.

It turns out, while we're happy to part with our money to buy expensive components to hit higher frame rates (and earn the right to brag about it), we're also just as happy to settle for less when a game does a lot of other things exceptionally well.

GTA 6 certainly does that. That's the impression I get from most members of the team that have played it so far. Though if Rockstar is listening, when you do get around to our precious PC version, we'd love nothing more than 4K60—maybe more.

I will no doubt appreciate frames above 100 fps when GTA 6 comes to PC. Heck, I'd even just appreciate going up to 60 fps. But in my handful of hours with the game thus far, I just have simply not been that bothered by it. Be it smart ways of masking low frames, or even just the slower, methodical control approach of the game, I'm less frustrated with my PS5 running the game at around 30 fps than I was recently playing Phantom Blade Zero at well above 40 fps on a handheld PC.

Maybe that's down to the world having a little bit of magic to it, maybe it's the engrossing tone and atmosphere, maybe it's just because it looks so darn pretty. Maybe it's because I haven't got to the game's most hectic moments yet and haven't really needed to hit a headshot with my console unable to keep up with me. I'll tell you how I'm getting on in another fifty hours. Cool, see you in three days, then?

I was dreading playing GTA 6 on my OG PS5—a dusty ornament that's been chilling out in my living room this last year doing absolutely nothing. I've got a nice gaming PC in my office (RTX 4090, Intel i9 13900K, 32 GB RAM), so it's been a long time since I've had to deal with games dipping below 80 fps. I have been spoiled.

The second I got to control Lucia, my fears seemed justified. Everything just felt sluggish. But that feeling didn't last. I played GTA 6 for around 5 hours last night (I am very tired) and I haven't thought about the frame rate once since that initial section. Whether I'm getting into shootouts with coke smugglers, speeding through the Keys at night, or bouncing around at sea, GTA 6 looks great and feels great.

I can still tell this isn't 60 fps, but it is smooth.

I can still tell this isn't 60 fps, but it is smooth. I'm sure I've encountered drops, but crucially I haven't noticed them. Sure, it's inevitably going to look better and run better on PC, but the lower performance on my PS5 quickly ceased to be an issue, and I'm not regretting playing it on console.

GTA 6 is the kind of game where an uncapped framerate would be nice, but it doesn't feel essential. Like Red Dead Redemption 2 before it—a game I also played at 30 fps before it launched on PC—its pacing is measured. It feels designed around the limitations of the consoles it's launching on, prioritising detail and depth over twitch-based combat and precise interaction. It's exactly what I'd expect from a modern Rockstar game. Also like Red Dead Redemption 2 before it, I still feel the sense of longing for what this game will look like on PC. Make no mistake: the version currently available is a preview for what GTA 6 will be at its best. It's great, but those who can wait will be treated to a superior experience.

It's also possible that the 30 fps cap will feel more restrictive once the online mode arrives—whenever that will be, and in whatever form it takes. It's one thing to handle a lower framerate within Rockstar's meticulously created campaign. It's quite another in a lobby of other players. If GTA 6's multiplayer is even half as chaotic as the current GTA Online, every frame is going to count.

As I was booting up GTA 6, I was expecting to be annoyed by the game's paltry frame rate. And I was—at first. Much like Fraser, during the opening scene with Lucia, I saw my fears come to life on the big screen in front of me. Objects juddering and blurring as I swung my camera around in the cramped cell. Did I just waste £80 on GTA 6 on PS5 when I should've held my nerve for the PC version?

Truth is, the frame rate has had nowhere near as much of a negative impact on my experience while I've been traversing the Floridian wilds as Jason. In part, I think that's because there's a lot more going on, as cars, shops, people, and poultry fly past me as I break most state, federal and ethical laws. That reduces the chance of my eyes fixating on any one object and noticing the adverse effects of the game's lower fps, or the ways Rockstar has gone about covering for it.

Low fps is one thing, but motion blur is the devil.

Low fps is one thing, but motion blur is the devil. That's not just my opinion, that's been scientifically verified (sorta) to be the opinion of PC Gamer readers. Admittedly, some motion blur may be required when the frame rate is this low, so I have played around with a few settings in GTA 6 to find the perfect balance. I'd heard through the grapevine that higher-than-default motion blur (default is 3, goes up to 10) may be preferential to reduce the more obvious juddering that is present at low fps, but whoever says that is no friend of mine. I've landed on setting motion blur to 1 on the standard PS5, as it feels the cleanest overall. I wouldn't blame anyone for turning it off entirely, especially on a more powerful console where the frame rate may not dip as much.

Of course, I do agree with the rest of this lot: in an ideal world, playing the PC version, I'd be pushing a much higher frame rate with motion blur banished to the abyss where it belongs, and a full selection of graphics settings to tinker with to my liking. Yet, to my surprise, I'm not as much of a console version curmudgeon as I thought I'd be.

Is the low frame rate noticeable? Yep. Would it be better at a higher frame rate? Also yep. Is the low frame rate a detriment to my overall enjoyment of GTA 6? Only a smidge.

I don't consider myself much of a framerate snob, but I'll admit I was side-eyeing GTA 6's 30fps just a little bit. Well, that was before the game came out. Now that I have my hands on it, with roughly six hours spent lollygagging around Leonida? I'm hardly noticing it, though I'll most definitely be appreciating a smoother experience once the PC version rolls around.

Like Jacob said, motion blur definitely seems to be masking it somewhat—and I am traditionally a motion blur hater, so it's taken a little getting used to—but I'm genuinely pleasantly surprised at the balance Rockstar has managed to strike between a smooth performance and a dense, rich world.

GTA 6 taught me that I don't much care about frame rates as much as I expected. I got to start playing it a few weeks ago and didn't have anyone to compare notes with, and my first thought was: Huh, they got it to run at 60 fps after all! It all felt very smooth, even when I realized it was 30 fps after all. It was only a bit later I started noticing very occasional drops, like while driving during a gradual lighting chance from day to night.

But that's really infrequent. I think it being consistent is key. I'm on a PS5 Slim, by the way, not a Pro. That's not to say I still can't wait to see it at higher frame rates when it finally gets to PC. But 30 fps feels mostly fine for the time being.

It was actually spending a lot of time playing with handheld gaming PCs and laptops with integrated graphics that reminded me I shouldn't give as much of a shit about frame rate as I do. Largely that obsession is born of having high-end hardware sat in my desktop PC, but when crashing around with a range of handhelds I'm reminded of the old days when 30 fps was a target for PC games, too.

It's also reminded me that it really depends on the game engine, as well. Not every 30 fps game looks the same as other 30 fps games. And Rockstar has obviously worked incredibly hard to make sure that 30 fps looks as good as it possible can. Otherwise why would that be a solid target for all four of the console platforms it's released on?

For the most part Rockstar has done a great job of keeping things smooth.

I've been playing GTA 6 on the Xbox Series X, which does suffer from the odd dip in frame rate, too—though oddly I've only really noticed it during canned animations the characters do starting certain actions, such as opening the trunk of a car or pulling something out of it. But for the most part Rockstar has done a great job of keeping things smooth. And not just by using motion blur. For the record, I'm running that at 0 and have not looked back.

I'm less happy about the vignetting that I'm getting around the darkened edges of the screen, but I'm playing it blown up on a 4K projector so I've got plenty of screen real estate to enjoy. And I have been, thoroughly enjoying it, I mean. The frame rate, for me, hasn't got in the way once.

#3675. After Grand Theft Auto 6's launch, players are in love with wacky criminality, in-game social media, and animal fatalities

With Grand Theft Auto 6 launching late last night (unless you're in New Zealand, in-person or otherwise), players have been flocking to online spaces to share their favourite moments. So far, slapstick violence, animal fatalities, and the in-game social media have won the hearts of many.

The game, a vast open world in which crime and violence may in fact pay, obviously allows players to get into brawls with the denizens of Vice City. While this can of course be brutal, many of these scuffles have a capacity for grand comedy.

GTA 6 is finally here, and I'm probably not alone in being tired after crashing around Leonida in an off-brand El Camino all night, blasting everything from Drake and Young Thug to Lana Del Rey and King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard. One thing no one is doing, however, is listening to Doja Cat, because the Paint the Town Red rapper is nowhere to be seen in the new biggest game in the world. As a FOMO sufferer myself, I can understand being a little salty about that, but Doja Cat is straight-up crashing out on Twitter.

"I would’ve loved to have my music on gta6 i’m so fuckin bitter," she writes at the beginning of a tweeting tirade against Rockstar. I say tirade, but it's really just three extremely sharply worded posts about not being in GTA 6.

"@RockstarGames eat my dick all yall i love your stupid fuckin bitch ass game," she says in a pretty dramatic escalation. And, finally, "@RockstarGames you broke my heart pinche culero," Doja Cat says, using the Spanish phrase for (roughly) "fucking jerk," as the slightly less explicit interpretation.

I would’ve loved to have my music on gta6 i’m so fuckin bitter.November 19, 2026

@RockstarGames eat my dick all yall i love your stupid fuckin bitch ass gameNovember 19, 2026

@RockstarGames you broke my heart pinche culeroNovember 19, 2026

It's clear Doja Cat is a big fan of Rockstar and GTA; only someone with a deep love or passion for someone or something can feel this kind of pain.

Also, the rapper is a known shitposter, so this probably isn't anywhere near as deep as it may appear without context. I won't lie though, Doja Cat definitely has a few bangers I wouldn't mind hearing in a future GTA 6 update. Dumb headline pun aside, Paint the Town Red seems like a song that was literally written to be included in a GTA game.

#3673. GTA 6 developers at Rockstar are worried about being laid off after shipping "the biggest game of all time"

Rockstar has successfully shipped Grand Theft Auto 6, after years of work and more than a billion dollars spent. GTA 6 is already one of the highest-rated games ever - Eurogamer awarded it five stars in our GTA 6 review - and it's expected to be among the most successful, best-selling games ever.

But that may not be enough to prevent layoffs at Rockstar, some people working within the studio fear. Nestor Uriarte, an animation programmer at Rockstar North, wrote about their concern for their job and those of their colleagues in an article on The Guardian.

"After the big day, we have had no indication that layoffs are coming, but it's hard not to worry about what the future holds," Uriarte wrote. "It says a lot about the industry that even my colleagues and I, working on the biggest game of all time, are worried about getting laid off. But the truth is that workers across the sector are helpless to resist the waves of redundancies crashing around us, until we get organised."

Uriarte's piece comes as Rockstar staff's efforts to establish a union reach a critical point. A tribunal between the studio and fired IWBG union members just concluded, though the verdict may not arrive for many weeks or months.

Rockstar's UK studios are currently voting on recognising an official Rockstar workers union. Uriarte is in support of it and has urged colleagues to vote in favour of it. Results of that vote are expected today.

"Winning union recognition would be a huge step forward in securing a meaningful say over our conditions at Rockstar, but its significance would reach far beyond that," Uriarte pointed out.

"As one of the biggest and most influential game studios in the world, what happens here could open the door for other workers across the UK to imagine an alternative future for the industry - one in which workers' voices are taken into account more."

Across its 12 offices around the world, Rockstar's headcount grew to 4,711 during GTA 6's development - double its size when it released Red Dead Redemption 2.

As popular and profitable as Rockstar's games are, the company has initiated layoffs in the past after shipping a major project. While there's no way of knowing whether the same is going to happen for GTA 6, the justifiable concerns - given the current state of the industry - are there. According to the ASGC Games Industry Layoffs Tracker, more than 12,000 developers have lost their jobs this year so far, up from more than 9,000 people last year.
